summaries.example: Imagine the sentence “Every cat is an animal.” Now replace “cat” with “dog.” The new sentence, “Every dog is an animal,” is also true. Bolzano studied what happens when we replace important ideas in a sentence. If every suitable replacement keeps the sentence true, the sentence has a special kind of logical strength.
summaries.summary: Bernard Bolzano was a priest, teacher, mathematician, and philosopher who worked in many fields. He is especially important for his ideas about logic. He said that meanings and propositions should be distinguished from the words and thoughts used to express or understand them. A proposition can be true even when nobody knows it. Bolzano also tried to keep logic apart from psychology, because logical truth should not depend on a person’s feelings or changing thoughts. His method of idea-variation tested a proposition by replacing some of its ideas with others. This helped him explain logical truth and logical consequence, which is when a conclusion must be true whenever its starting statements are true. He also developed influential ideas about mathematics, probability, ethics, and the foundations of science.
key_ideas: Bolzano thought logic should be kept separate from psychology. Logic studies meanings and relations that do not depend on what one person happens to think.
He distinguished propositions from sentences. A sentence is written or spoken; a proposition is the meaning that the sentence expresses.
He used idea-variation to test reasoning by changing non-logical ideas and checking which replacements remain true.
He also studied mathematics, religion, ethics, politics, and science. His work tried to find clear reasons and better foundations for knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bolzano showed that questions about meaning, truth, and reasoning can be studied carefully. His work helped point toward later developments in modern logic and mathematics. His example also shows how one person can connect different subjects while asking the same basic question: What makes a claim well supported?

important_terms.definition: A statement that can be true or false, whether or not anyone has said or thought it.
A basic meaning or concept, such as “cat,” “animal,” or “red.”
A careful way to study reasoning and how statements support one another.
Replacing one idea in a proposition with another idea of the same kind.
A statement that is true because of its logical pattern, not because of a special fact.

summaries.example: Consider “Every German philosopher is European.” If we vary the idea “philosopher,” many replacements produce true statements, provided the subject class is not empty: “Every German mathematician is European,” for example, follows from the fact that Germans are Europeans. But changing “European” to “American” does not preserve truth. Bolzano’s method asks which parts can be varied while a proposition remains true. When all extra-logical simple ideas are varied and the truth-pattern is preserved, the proposition is logically true. This differs from a merely factual generalization, whose validity depends on how the world happens to be.
summaries.summary: Bernard Bolzano (1781–1848) was a Prague-based priest, professor, mathematician, and philosopher whose work ranged from logic and mathematics to ethics, religion, political philosophy, aesthetics, and the philosophy of science. His major logical project, developed especially in Theory of Science, began with a sharp separation between logic and psychology. Bolzano held that propositions and ideas are objective items: propositions are true or false, while ideas are parts of propositions and are neither true nor false. Sentences and judgments are their linguistic and mental counterparts, not identical with them. This framework supported his claim that truth can be independent of anyone’s knowledge. Bolzano analyzed propositions through a subject-predicate scheme, though the source notes that this approach remained limited and lacked a general organizing device like later function-argument theories. His most innovative logical tool was idea-variation. By replacing selected extra-logical ideas with suitable alternatives, one can study a proposition’s form. A proposition is logically true when its relevant logical variants preserve truth in the appropriate way; logical consequence is similarly defined through variations of premises and conclusion. These definitions are complicated by empty subject ideas and by purely logical propositions, so Bolzano gives priority to propositional forms in addressing those cases. He further distinguished material consequence, which depends on factual content, from logical consequence, and entailment, which concerns an objective ground or explanation. key_ideas: Bolzano’s broad conception of logic included the organization of sciences, foundations, knowledge, discovery, and the study of science, not only formal inference.
He separated objective propositions and ideas from their mental appearances and linguistic expressions. This distinction was central to his opposition to psychologism.
His subject-predicate analysis treated propositions as having a common structure, while also handling negation, generality, existence claims, and propositions about propositions.
Idea-variation made it possible to define logical properties semantically: the relevant question is how truth changes when non-logical components are substituted.
Bolzano distinguished material consequence from logical consequence. A conclusion may follow because of particular facts without following solely from logical form.
He also distinguished entailment, which explains why a conclusion is true or gives its objective ground, from logical consequence, which concerns preservation of truth.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bolzano stands at an important point in the history of analytic philosophy, logic, and mathematics. His insistence that truth and consequence are not merely psychological events anticipates a central concern of later objective and semantic approaches to logic. Idea-variation also offers an early way to study logical form by examining what remains stable across substitutions. At the same time, the source notes important limitations: his ontology of propositions and ideas is not fully clear, and his subject-predicate analysis does not provide a complete general system. Studying both the achievements and the unresolved problems helps explain how logical theories develop.

important_terms.definition: An objective meaning that can be expressed by language and grasped by thought; in Bolzano’s theory, ideas are parts of propositions.
An objective bearer of truth or falsity, distinct from a spoken or written sentence and from a mental judgment.
The view that logical properties should not be defined by facts about human psychological processes.
A systematic replacement of selected extra-logical ideas in a proposition by ideas from the same semantic category.
A proposition whose relevant variants remain true in the required way when its extra-logical ideas are varied.
A relation in which a conclusion is true under every relevant variation that makes the premises true.
A relation in which premises provide the objective ground or reason why a conclusion is true; it is distinct from logical consequence.
A proposition’s being true or false because its subject idea has objects and those objects have the attributed property.

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “Every square has four sides.” You can replace “square” with “triangle,” but the result is false. You can replace it with “rectangle,” and the result is true. Bolzano would ask which parts of the statement can be changed while its pattern stays reliable. A statement such as “Every square has four sides” depends partly on what squares are. A statement such as “A thing is either red or not red” seems to depend more on the logical structure. Idea-variation helps compare these cases.
summaries.summary: Bernard Bolzano was a philosopher, mathematician, Catholic priest, and teacher whose ideas covered many areas. The SEP entry gives special attention to his logic. Bolzano thought logic should be objective, so it should not be defined by what happens in individual minds. He therefore distinguished a proposition from a sentence and from a judgment. A sentence is a group of words, a judgment is a mental act of accepting a proposition, and a proposition is the meaning that can be true or false. Bolzano argued that some truths are independent of human knowledge: a mathematical theorem, for example, did not become true only when someone discovered it. He also proposed a realm of objective ideas and propositions, although the source notes that his account of this realm remains unclear in some respects. Bolzano analyzed propositions using a subject-and-predicate pattern, often expressed as “A has b.” He used it to discuss ordinary, negative, general, and existence claims. His most important logical innovation was idea-variation. This method replaces one or more non-logical ideas with others that fit the same role. If every relevant replacement remains true, the original has a kind of universal validity. When all the relevant non-logical parts are varied, this method helps define logical truth. Bolzano also explained logical consequence by asking whether every variation that makes the premises true makes the conclusion true. Material consequence is different: a conclusion can follow from particular facts, such as a fact about Germans and Europeans. Entailment is different again because it concerns the objective ground or explanation of a conclusion. key_ideas: Bolzano was a wide-ranging thinker who worked in mathematics, logic, theology, ethics, politics, and the philosophy of science.
He argued that logic should not be mixed up with psychology. People may think about a proposition, but the proposition itself is not the same as a thought in someone’s mind.
He believed there are objective propositions and ideas. A proposition may be true even if everyone is unaware of it.
His analysis often represented propositions as something like “A has property b.” He used this structure to discuss general statements, negative statements, and claims about whether things exist.
Idea-variation examines what happens when selected ideas are replaced. It helps separate truths that depend on particular facts from truths connected with logical form.
Bolzano distinguished logical consequence from material consequence and from entailment. These relations answer different questions about reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bolzano helps us see that reasoning involves several different questions. Is a statement true? Does it follow from a set of statements? Is it true because of logical form, or because of facts about the world? Does an argument merely establish its conclusion, or does it explain why the conclusion holds? His distinctions became useful for later thinking about semantics, logic, probability, and scientific explanation. His career also shows how mathematical methods such as indirect proof and induction can influence philosophical arguments, even when those arguments may later be criticized.

important_terms.definition: The meaning of a statement, considered separately from the particular words used to express it.
A meaning or concept that can be part of a proposition, such as “square” or “four-sided.”
The study of rules for reasoning and of how knowledge and sciences should be organized.
A method of testing a proposition by replacing some of its ideas with suitable alternatives.
A proposition whose truth survives all the relevant replacements of its non-logical ideas.
A connection in which true premises guarantee a true conclusion through their logical structure.
A connection in which a conclusion follows from particular facts or laws, even if the connection is not purely logical.
The objective reason or ground that makes a conclusion true, rather than merely a pattern that preserves truth.
